author: amy-carmichael
fields.title: If
fields.description: IF, is a heartfelt devotional in which Amy Carmichael uses a series of probing “ifs” to reveal how easily the heart falls short of Christ-like love. Born from deep personal reflection, the book challenges readers to examine hidden motives and measure their lives against the self-giving love of the Cross. Yet its message is full of hope, pointing to God’s grace as the source of true transformation and deeper love.

fields.title: The Love of Jesus—what It Is
fields.body_html:
There are times when something comes into our lives so charged with love that it seems, for a moment, to open the Eternal to us—or at least to open something of the Eternal. Of all eternal realities, the greatest is love.

It may come as a small and deeply personal touch upon us or our affairs, as gentle as the morning breeze moving through the leaves of a tree—something that cannot be captured or fully explained to another. Yet we know it is our Lord. And then perhaps the room we are in, with its furniture, books, and flowers, feels less real than His presence, and the heart is drawn into that sweetness of which the old hymn speaks: The love of Jesus—what it is; none but His loved ones know. Or it may be the human love around us, enfolding us like warm summer seas and bringing rest to the whole being. Can we ever stop wondering at the love of those who walk with us? And then, suddenly, we recognise our Lord in them. It is His love that they pour out upon us. O Love of God, made visible in those who love You, we worship You.

Or—perhaps not often, for a certain dimness seems more fitting for us in this life, yet sometimes, because our Lord is rich in mercy—we are allowed to lift our eyes and glimpse the love of God itself. And even then, how little we truly see. “That you may be able to comprehend the breadth and length and depth and height, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” —the words themselves reach beyond us.

What do we truly understand? What do we really know? Humbled and brought low, we take refuge in the Rock and bow in the dust before the glory of love in all its majesty—the love whose sign and symbol is the Cross.

And then the question breaks through, sharp and searching: What do I know of Calvary love?

fields.title: What Do I Know of Calvary Love?
fields.body_html:
If I do not have compassion on my fellow servant, just as my Lord had compassion on me, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I belittle those whom I am called to serve, speaking of their weaknesses, perhaps in contrast to what I think of as my strengths; if I adopt a superior attitude, forgetting, “Who made you different? And what do you have that you did not receive?” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I can easily discuss the shortcomings and sins of others; if I can speak casually even of a child’s wrongdoing, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I find myself almost carelessly taking failures for granted—“Oh, that’s what they always do,” or “Of course she talks like that; he always acts like that”—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I enjoy a joke at another’s expense; if I slight another in conversation, or even in thought, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I can write an unkind letter, speak an unkind word, or think an unkind thought without grief and shame, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If, when troubling things happen, I feel far more for my own anxiety than for the wounded heart of my Saviour, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I know little of His tenderness ( “The Lord turned and looked at Peter” ); if I know little of His courageous hopefulness for the truly humble and repentant ( “He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs’” ), then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I deal with wrongdoing for any reason other than that implied in the words, “From His right hand went a fiery law for them. Yes, He loved the people” ; if I can rebuke without inner pain, then I know nothing of Calvary love. If, when dealing with one who does not respond, I grow weary of the strain and step out from under the burden, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot be like the father who did not soften the hardships of the far country; if, in this sense, I refuse to allow the law of God— “the way of transgressors is hard” —to take effect because it pains me to watch that law at work, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am troubled by the reproach and misunderstanding that may follow action taken for the good of souls for whom I must give account, if I cannot commit the matter to God and go on in peace and silence, remembering Gethsemane and the Cross, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot hear “the sound of the rain” long before it falls, and, going up to some spiritual high place as near to God as I can, lack the faith to wait there with my face between my knees— though six times or sixty times I am told, “There is nothing” —until at last “a little cloud arises out of the sea,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

1 Kings 18:41 If my attitude towards one who has disappointed me is fear rather than faith; if I say, “Just what I expected,” when a fall occurs, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I do not look with eyes of hope upon all in whom there is even the faintest beginning, as our Lord did when, just after His disciples had argued about who should be greatest, He softened His rebuke with those melting words, “You are those who have continued with Me in My trials,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I hold against another a sin that has been confessed, repented of, and forsaken, allowing the memory of it to colour my thoughts and feed my suspicions, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I do not have the patience of my Saviour with souls who grow slowly; if I know little of that painful travail until Christ is fully formed in them, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I sympathise weakly with weakness, saying to one who is turning back from the Cross, “Spare yourself” ; if I withhold the bracing sympathy and the brave, strengthening word of true comradeship, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot keep silence about a disappointing soul—unless speaking is necessary for that soul’s good or for the good of others—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I can wound another by speaking truthfully without careful preparation of spirit, and without being wounded far more deeply myself, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am afraid to speak the truth for fear of losing affection, or of hearing, “You do not understand,” or of losing my reputation for kindness; if I place my own good name above another’s highest good, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am content to heal a wound lightly, saying “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace; if I forget the piercing command, “Let love be without hypocrisy,” and blunt the edge of truth by speaking smooth things instead of right things, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I fear holding another to the highest calling because it is easier not to do so, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cling to choices simply because they are my choices; if I give any room to personal likes and dislikes, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I put my own happiness before the wellbeing of the work entrusted to me; if, though I have received this ministry and so much mercy, I grow weary and faint, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am gentle with myself and slide easily into the habit of self-pity and self-sympathy; if I do not, by God’s grace, practise endurance, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I myself dominate my thoughts; if my mind revolves around me; if I am so occupied with myself that I rarely have “a heart at leisure from itself,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If, the moment I sense self crossing my threshold, I do not shut the door—and by the power of Him who works in us both to will and to act, keep that door firmly shut—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot happily take the second place—or the twentieth; if I cannot take the first without drawing attention to my unworthiness, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If, when I discover something that has puzzled others, I forget Him who reveals deep and hidden things, who knows what lies in darkness and brings it to light; if I forget that He granted that insight to His most unworthy servant, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot rest under what I do not understand, forgetting the words, “Blessed is anyone who is not offended because of Me,” or if I allow even a shadow of resentment to enter, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I do not give a friend the benefit of the doubt, but choose the worst interpretation rather than the best of what is said or done, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I take offence easily, if I am content to continue in a cold unfriendliness when friendship could be restored, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If a sudden jolt can make me speak an impatient, unloving word, then I know nothing of Calvary love.* A cup filled to the brim with sweet water cannot spill even one drop of bitter water, however suddenly it is shaken.

If I feel wronged when others accuse me of things I do not recognise in myself, forgetting that my sinless Saviour walked this road to the very end, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I feel bitterness towards those who condemn me, as I think, unjustly—forgetting that if they knew me as I know myself they would condemn me far more—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I say, “Yes, I forgive, but I cannot forget,” as though the God who washes all the sands of every shore each day could not cleanse such memories from my mind, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If someone whose help I greatly need seems content to build with wood, hay, and straw instead of gold, silver, and precious stones, and I hesitate to obey the light given to me and go on without that help because so few will understand, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If the care of a soul—or a community—is entrusted to me, and I allow it to be weakened because the voice of the world, even my immediate Christian world, is loud in my ears, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I can best help others by doing work that undiscerning people call “not spiritual,” and inwardly I resist because what I truly crave is not the spiritual but the interesting and exciting, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If monotony tests me and I cannot endure drudgery; if slow minds irritate me and small disturbances unsettle me; if I magnify the trifles of life, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am careless about the comfort or feelings of others, or about their small weaknesses; if I overlook their minor hurts and miss chances to smooth their path; if I make the gentle running of daily life more difficult, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If interruptions irritate me and private worries make me impatient; if I cast a shadow over others because I myself feel shadowed, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If souls suffer beside me and I scarcely notice, because the spirit of discernment is lacking in me, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If there is any reserve in my giving to Him who loved me enough to give His dearest for me; if there is a hidden “but” in my prayer— “anything but that, Lord” —then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I become entangled in any inordinate affection; if things, places, or people hold me back from obedience to my Lord, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If something I am asked to do for another feels heavy, and yielding to inner reluctance I avoid doing it, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If praise lifts me up and blame casts me down; if I cannot rest under misunderstanding without defending myself; if I love being loved more than loving, being served more than serving, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I long to be the one who leads a captive soul into freedom, rather than caring only that it is set free; if I nurse disappointment when I fail instead of praying that another may be given the word of release, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I want to be known as the one who did what proved right, or as the one who first suggested it, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I do not forget such a trifle as personal success, so that it scarcely enters my mind—or, if it does, is never allowed to linger; if the taste of spiritual flattery is sweet to me, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If it is not simple and natural for me to say, “Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If, in the fellowship of service, I seek to bind a friend to myself in a way that leaves others feeling excluded; if my friendships do not draw others in but remain self-centred, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I refuse to allow one dear to me to suffer for Christ’s sake; if I do not see such suffering as the highest honour offered to any follower of the Crucified; if I step into a place that belongs to Christ alone, making myself essential to a soul instead of leading it to cling to Him, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If my interest in the work of others is lukewarm; if I think mainly in terms of my own work; if the burdens of others are not my burdens, nor their joys my joys, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If an answer comes to prayer that I did not expect, though I believed I truly meant it, and I shrink back from it; if the burden my Lord asks me to carry is not the one I would choose, and I fret inwardly instead of welcoming His will, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I avoid being “ploughed under,” with all that such ploughing involves—rough handling, loneliness, uncongenial situations, unfamiliar tests—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I question why something difficult is allowed and urge prayer that it be removed; if I cannot be trusted with disappointment or go on in peace amid mystery, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I exaggerate anything appointed to me, magnifying it in my own mind or subtly in the minds of others; if I allow it to appear “hard” ; if I look back with longing on what once was and linger in memory’s side paths until my usefulness is weakened, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If the love that “alone makes light of every heavy thing and bears evenly every uneven thing” is not my heart’s desire, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I refuse to be a grain of wheat that falls into the ground and dies— separated from all that once sustained it —then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I ask to be spared trial rather than delivered through it to the praise of His glory; if I forget that the way of the Cross leads to the Cross and not to a bed of flowers; if I shape my life—or even my thinking—so that I am surprised when the path is rough, despite the command, “Do not think it strange,” “Count it all joy,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If the ultimate demand, the hardest demand, cannot be made of me; if my fellow workers hesitate to ask it and turn to someone else, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I desire any place on earth other than the dust at the foot of the Cross, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

What I do not know, teach me, O Lord my God.

fields.title: What I Do Not Know, Teach Me, O Lord My God
fields.body_html:
I have felt these words to be scorching as I have written them. Yet it has been pressed upon me that, despite all our hymns and prayers—so many of them prayers for love—it is possible to be content with the shallows of love, if indeed such shallows deserve to be called love at all.

(Perhaps prayer often needs to be followed by a pause, so that we may have time to open our hearts to what we have asked for. We rush too quickly from one prayer to another, without waiting for the inward word that says, “I have heard you, My child.” ) The more we ponder our Lord’s words about love, and the burning words the Spirit inspired His followers to write, the more keenly we become aware of our deadly lack. The searchlight of the Spirit exposes us to ourselves, and such a revelation leaves us appalled. How can even He, who is the God of all patience, have patience with us? Like Job, we loathe ourselves and repent in dust and ashes.

But the light is not turned upon us to strip us of hope. There is a lifting up. If only we truly desire to be cleansed from self, with its entangling nets, its subtleties and disguises—its falsehoods, its easy substitution of brass for gold, as the Tamil saying puts it—if, hating unlove from the depths of our hearts, we cry out to be delivered, then our God will indeed be to us a God of deliverances.

No vision of the night, no spoken word, can reveal the depth of longing with which divine love waits until the heart, weary and sick of itself, turns to its Lord and says, “Take full possession.”

There is no need to plead with God to fill us with His love, as though He were reluctant. He is as willing as light is willing to flood a room opened to its brightness, as willing as water is to flow into an emptied channel. Love presses around us on every side, like the air we breathe. Cease to resist, and at once love takes possession.

As the fifteenth-century poem Quia Amore Langues says: Long and love thou never so high, my love is more than thine may be. More—far more. For just as His abundance of pardon surpasses our ability to tell it, so does His abundance of love. It is as far as the east is from the west, as high as the heavens are above the earth. Words fail us. Love rises beyond them all.

To look at ourselves leads only to despair. Thank God, the Blood cleanses.

If you are defiled, I will make you clean; if you are sick, I will heal you—have you ever found love so real?

Never, Lord—never.

Sometimes, when we are distressed by past failure and tormented by fear of failing again should we set our faces once more toward Jerusalem, nothing helps so much as allowing a familiar Scripture to sink into us and become part of our being. The words “grace upon grace” have helped me ever since I read, in a small old book by Bishop Moule, an explanation that opened their meaning to me—for until then, I had not understood them.

He explains that “for” means simply instead . The image is one of continual supply, an unceasing exchange—a constant replacement as needs arise.

He writes of a river: stand by its bank and watch the waters flow. A minute passes, then another.

Is it still the same river? Yes. But is it the same water? No. The water that passed a moment ago has moved on; fresh water has taken its place— water instead of water . So it is hour by hour, year by year, century by century: one river, ever-changing waters, living and not stagnant, because within the unchanging identity there is constant renewal. Grace takes the place of grace—and love the place of love—ever new, ever old, ever the same, ever fresh and young, through Christ.

There is no power strong enough to hold us together as a company and give life to all we do except this one power: love. That is why love is constantly attacked, for without it we become sounding brass and clanging cymbals.

This explains why, from time to time, those who desire to live the life of love are compelled to seek the searching and cleansing of the Spirit of God—first in the secret places of our own hearts, and then together. And we know how graciously God has met us, so that although we must always say, “Not that I have already attained,” yet by His enabling we press on.

There is another reason why the enemy attacks love. Something may occur on the outermost edge of our work that is, in a sense, the reflection of something hidden in the heart of one at the very centre. I have seen this again and again. It may never have been expressed in word or action; eye did not see it, ear did not hear it. Yet spiritual influences move where sight and sound do not reach. Unlove in any one of us—or even the absence of that quality of love we have been considering—can allow a slow stain to spread, until it reaches a soul at a moment of weakness, with harm that cannot be undone.

O Lord, forgive—Your very nature is mercy. Restore to me the comfort of Your help. Be pleased to deliver me, O Lord my God.

The way of love is never the easy way. If our hearts are set on walking in it, we must be prepared to suffer. “It was the way the Master went; should not the servant tread it still?” There may be times when we are shut in by circumstances that drain natural love until we feel as dry as grass on an Indian hillside under a blazing sun.

We have laboured for someone dear to us without ever thinking of it as labour. We have spent reserves of health that can never be recovered, yet we never counted the cost, nor would we have done so, because we loved so deeply. Our one hope was that the one so cherished would become a blessing to others—but it did not happen.

Slowly and unwillingly we become aware of a strange lack of response in the one for whom nothing had seemed too much; of a coldness that chills, a hardness that pushes away the heart that nearly broke to save that life from destruction.

Then—only those who have passed through such an hour will understand—a fear more terrible than pain grips us: Is the love of the years slipping away? *“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”—*is that fading from us? *“Love never fails”—*is love failing now?

Shall we meet lovelessness with lovelessness?

In such an hour, words written long ago gave voice to a desperate prayer: Deep calls to deep, O Lord, within me; Gathering strength, I come, Lord, to You. Jesus of Calvary, wounded for me, Ask what You will—but give me love.

Yes—ask what You will. Take hopes, joys, even the rewards of human affection, but do not let love depart. Nothing ordinary can meet this call; nothing in me is enough. O Lord of Love and Lord of Pain, abound in me in love. Love through me, Love of God.

Our dear Lord listens to prayers that rise from honest lips. For our comfort it is written that He causes those who love Him to inherit substance—the marvellous substance of “grace instead of grace,” the unending gift of His fullness. This grace is not an impersonal thing, but God Himself at work within us—the Lord active in the deepest springs of thought and will. God is love; therefore love itself is this blessed substance which the children of the Father inherit.

Once again, the river speaks. The empty riverbed inherits the water that pours into it from the heights. It does not create the water; it only receives it. Its channels are filled, its pools overflow, and the land is refreshed. So it is with us. Our treasuries of time—our years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes—are filled with the flowing wealth of love, so that we may bless others.

Who could have imagined such joy for us but He whose name is Love?

Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, according to the power at work within us—to Him be glory.

Let us end on a simple note. Let us listen to simple words. Our Lord speaks gently: “Trust Me, My child. Trust Me with a humbler heart and a fuller surrender to My will than ever before. Trust Me to pour My love through you, minute by minute. And if you become aware of anything that hinders that flow, do not wound My love by withdrawing in discouragement—for nothing hurts more than that. Draw closer. Come and hide in Me, even from yourself. Tell Me what troubles you. Trust Me to put My hand upon you and remove completely the boulder that has blocked the riverbed, and clear away the silt that has choked the channel. I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised. I will perfect what concerns you. Do not fear, child of My love—do not fear.”

And now, to gather all into one page: Beloved, let us love.

Lord, what is love?

Love is that which shaped My life, led Me to My Cross, and held Me upon it.

Love is that which will make it your joy to lay down your life for your brothers.

Lord, always give me this love.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for love, for they shall be filled.

END
fields.body_text: I have felt these words to be scorching as I have written them. Yet it has been pressed upon me that, despite all our hymns and prayers—so many of them prayers for love—it is possible to be content with the shallows of love, if indeed such shallows deserve to be called love at all. (Perhaps prayer often needs to be followed by a pause, so that we may have time to open our hearts to what we have asked for. We rush too quickly from one prayer to another, without waiting for the inward word that says, “I have heard you, My child.” ) The more we ponder our Lord’s words about love, and the burning words the Spirit inspired His followers to write, the more keenly we become aware of our deadly lack. The searchlight of the Spirit exposes us to ourselves, and such a revelation leaves us appalled. How can even He, who is the God of all patience, have patience with us? Like Job, we loathe ourselves and repent in dust and ashes. But the light is not turned upon us to strip us of hope. There is a lifting up. If only we truly desire to be cleansed from self, with its entangling nets, its subtleties and disguises—its falsehoods, its easy substitution of brass for gold, as the Tamil saying puts it—if, hating unlove from the depths of our hearts, we cry out to be delivered, then our God will indeed be to us a God of deliverances.
